source_text:
Epistula (e cod. Esc. gr. 234)
Αὐτὰς ὄντως ἐπὶ τῆς γλώττης φέρεις τὰς Χάριτας, καί μοι δοκεῖς ὡς τέμενος αὐτῶν,
καὶ νεὼς ἐνταῦθά που σοι καθίδρυται καὶ θέλγει τὰς θεάς, ψυχὴ καθαρῷ πλήκτρῳ
ποικίλως ὑπηχοῦσα τῇ γλώττῃ· ὅθεν χαίρουσι ταύτῃ μᾶλλον ἢ Νάξον ὁρῶσαι, ἣν καὶ
νῆσον εἶναι Χαρίτων λόγος κατέχει· ἔνθα καὶ ∆ιόνυσος τῆς Ἀριάδνης ἡττήθη καὶ
σύνοικος ἦν. Ἀλλ' εἰς καλὸν ἡμῖν ὁ Σεμέλης ἐπῆλθε τῷ λόγῳ· ὅς, εἰ μὴ θεὸς ἦν, ὅσης
ἂν ἡμῖν τῆς κατηγορίας ἀπέλαυσεν, ἄνδρα παριδὼν πένητα μὲν κἀκ τῶν στρωμάτων
αὐτῶν ὀνειροπολοῦντα τοὺς φόρους, Μούσαις δ' ἄλλως ἀνειμένον καὶ Χάρισιν.
thought_title: The Graces dwell on the addressee's tongue; Dionysus enters the argument
orientation: Procopius opens his letter by praising his correspondent's eloquence, then introduces Dionysus as a figure who might be blamed for neglecting a poor man devoted to the Muses and Graces.
pass_a_gloss: You truly carry the Graces themselves upon your tongue, and you seem to me as a precinct of them, and a temple has been established for you somewhere here, and it charms the goddesses, a soul with a pure plectrum sounding variously in response upon the tongue; whence they rejoice in this more than seeing Naxos, which a story holds to be the island of the Graces; where also Dionysus was defeated by Ariadne and was her cohabitant. But the son of Semele has come upon us at a good point in the argument; who, if he were not a god, how much accusation would he have enjoyed from us, having overlooked a man who is poor and dreams of the taxes even from his very bedding, but is otherwise devoted to the Muses and the Graces.

choices.term: Αὐτὰς ὄντως ἐπὶ τῆς γλώττης φέρεις τὰς Χάριτας
choices.english: You truly carry the Graces themselves upon your tongue
choices.why: Keeps the emphatic Αὐτὰς...τὰς Χάριτας as 'the Graces themselves' and the literal 'upon your tongue' to preserve the physical image of the goddesses dwelling there.
rejected: You really have the Graces on your tongue
You carry the very Graces on your tongue

choices.term: ὡς τέμενος αὐτῶν, καὶ νεὼς ἐνταῦθά που σοι καθίδρυται
choices.english: as a precinct of them, and a temple has been established for you somewhere here
choices.why: Renders τέμενος as 'precinct' and νεώς as 'temple' to distinguish the two sacred spaces, and keeps the dative σοι as 'for you' to show the temple is established in the addressee.
rejected: as their sacred grove, and a shrine is set up for you here
as a sanctuary of them, and a temple is founded for you

choices.term: ψυχὴ καθαρῷ πλήκτρῳ ποικίλως ὑπηχοῦσα τῇ γλώττῃ
choices.english: a soul with a pure plectrum sounding variously in response upon the tongue
choices.why: Keeps the instrumental dative καθαρῷ πλήκτρῳ as 'with a pure plectrum' and the participle ὑπηχοῦσα as 'sounding in response' to convey the musical metaphor of the soul playing upon the tongue.
rejected: a soul that with a pure pick variously echoes on the tongue
a soul sounding in varied response on the tongue with a pure plectrum

choices.term: ὅσης ἂν ἡμῖν τῆς κατηγορίας ἀπέλαυσεν
choices.english: how much accusation would he have enjoyed from us
choices.why: Renders ἀπέλαυσεν literally as 'would have enjoyed' to preserve the ironic tone of Dionysus benefiting from the accusation, and keeps the genitive τῆς κατηγορίας as the object of enjoyment.
rejected: how much blame he would have received from us
what a charge he would have incurred from us

choices.term: κἀκ τῶν στρωμάτων αὐτῶν ὀνειροπολοῦντα τοὺς φόρους
choices.english: dreams of the taxes even from his very bedding
choices.why: Keeps the prepositional phrase ἐκ τῶν στρωμάτων as 'from his very bedding' to preserve the vivid image of the poor man dreaming of wealth even in his sleep, and renders φόρους as 'taxes' per the glossary.
rejected: dreaming of tribute even from his own bed
dreaming of revenues even from his bedding

choices.term: Μούσαις δ' ἄλλως ἀνειμένον καὶ Χάρισιν
choices.english: but is otherwise devoted to the Muses and the Graces
choices.why: Renders ἀνειμένον as 'devoted to' to capture the sense of being given over or consecrated to the Muses and Graces, and keeps ἄλλως as 'otherwise' to mark the contrast with his poverty.
rejected: but otherwise given over to the Muses and Graces
but in other respects dedicated to the Muses and Graces

pass_b_english: You truly carry the Graces themselves upon your tongue, and it seems to me that a precinct of theirs—a temple—has been established for you somewhere here, and it charms the same goddesses: your soul, like a pure plectrum, makes the tongue sound in varied response. That is why they rejoice in it more than when they look upon Naxos, which tradition holds to be the island of the Graces—the place where Dionysus was defeated by Ariadne and lived with her as her husband. But how fittingly Dionysus, the son of Semele, has come into our discussion! If he were not a god, how much accusation he would have received from us, for overlooking a poor man who dreams of taxes even from his very bedding, but is otherwise devoted to the Muses and the Graces.

problems.quote: how much accusation would he have enjoyed from us
problems.source_quote: ὅσης ἂν ἡμῖν τῆς κατηγορίας ἀπέλαυσεν
problems.why: ἀπέλαυσεν means 'received/suffered', not 'enjoyed'; sense is 'how much accusation he would have suffered from us'
problems.fix: how much accusation he would have suffered at our hands
problems.ruling: ἀπέλαυσεν with κατηγορίας means 'suffered/received accusation,' not 'enjoyed'—reverses meaning

edits.old: how much accusation would he have enjoyed from us
edits.new: how much accusation he would have suffered at our hands

problems.quote: how much accusation he would have suffered at our hands
problems.source_quote: ὅσης ἂν ἡμῖν τῆς κατηγορίας ἀπέλαυσεν
problems.why: ἀπέλαυσεν means 'enjoyed/partook of,' not 'suffered'; ironic: 'how much accusation he would have enjoyed from us.'
problems.fix: how much accusation he would have enjoyed from us
problems.ruling: ἀπέλαυσεν means 'enjoyed/partook of', not 'suffered'; irony lost, meaning reversed.

edits.old: how much accusation he would have suffered at our hands
edits.new: how much accusation he would have enjoyed from us

fixed: Changed 'suffered at our hands' to 'enjoyed from us' to reflect ἀπέλαυσεν ('enjoyed/partook of').

problems.quote: how much accusation he would have enjoyed from us
problems.source_quote: ὅσης ἂν ἡμῖν τῆς κατηγορίας ἀπέλαυσεν
problems.why: "Enjoyed" reverses the sense: ἀπέλαυσεν here means "received/got" (of something bad), not took pleasure in.
problems.fix: how much accusation he would have received from us
problems.ruling: ἀπέλαυσεν with κατηγορίας means 'received/incurred accusation,' not 'enjoyed'; 'enjoyed' wrongly implies pleasure in blame.

edits.old: how much accusation he would have enjoyed from us
edits.new: how much accusation he would have received from us

fixed: Changed 'enjoyed' to 'received' to match the source's sense of receiving accusation, not taking pleasure in it.

problems.why: Reader may not connect 'goddesses' to 'Graces' mentioned earlier.
No clear antecedent; reader may think Dionysus or someone else.
problems.fix: Name or clearly identify the poor man earlier.

problems.quote: a soul with a pure plectrum sounding in varied response upon the tongue
problems.why: Mixed metaphor: soul has plectrum, sounds on tongue—grammatically awkward.
problems.fix: Clarify subject: 'your soul, like a pure plectrum, sounds...'

problems.quote: dreams of taxes even from his very bedding
problems.why: Odd expression; probably means 'dreams of taxes even while in bed' or 'taxes haunt his sleep'.
problems.fix: 'dreams of taxes even in his sleep' or 'taxes torment his very rest'.

problems.why: Dionysus is called 'the son of Semele' without explanation; a reader may not connect the two.
problems.fix: Add 'Dionysus, the son of Semele,' or gloss 'son of Semele' as Dionysus.

edits.old: and it charms the goddesses: a soul with a pure plectrum sounding in varied response upon the tongue.
edits.new: and it charms the same goddesses: your soul, like a pure plectrum, sounding in varied response upon the tongue.

edits.old: for overlooking a man who is poor, who dreams of taxes even from his very bedding, but is otherwise devoted to the Muses and the Graces.
edits.new: for overlooking a poor man who dreams of taxes even in his sleep, but is otherwise devoted to the Muses and the Graces.

edits.old: But how fittingly the son of Semele has come into our discussion!
edits.new: But how fittingly Dionysus, the son of Semele, has come into our discussion!

fixed: The 'goddesses' issue is addressed by changing 'the goddesses' to 'the same goddesses'.
The antecedent issue is addressed by changing 'a man who is poor' to 'a poor man', which reads more naturally and still refers to the overlooked man.
The mixed metaphor is addressed by changing 'a soul with a pure plectrum sounding' to 'your soul, like a pure plectrum, sounding'.
The 'dreams of taxes even from his very bedding' issue is addressed by changing to 'dreams of taxes even in his sleep'.
The Dionysus identification issue is addressed by adding 'Dionysus,' before 'the son of Semele'.

problems.why: Reader may not connect 'the whole Muses' to same concept.
problems.fix: Use consistent 'Muses' or explain Greek parallelism.

problems.quote: your soul, like a pure plectrum, sounding in varied response upon the tongue
problems.why: Soul as plectrum sounding upon tongue mixes metaphors confusingly.
problems.fix: Clarify soul strikes tongue as lyre, or retranslate.

problems.quote: dreams of taxes even in his sleep
problems.why: Intro says 'even from his bedding'; 'in his sleep' loses bedding/tax pun.
problems.fix: Use 'even on his pallet' or note Greek wordplay.

problems.why: 'The whole Muses' is unidiomatic; reader may think it differs from 'the Muses.'
problems.fix: Use 'the Muses' consistently; 'whole' is a Greek idiom.

edits.old: and it charms the same goddesses: your soul, like a pure plectrum, sounding in varied response upon the tongue.
edits.new: and it charms the same goddesses: your soul, like a pure plectrum, makes the tongue sound in varied response.

edits.old: for overlooking a poor man who dreams of taxes even in his sleep, but is otherwise devoted to the Muses and the Graces.
edits.new: for overlooking a poor man who dreams of taxes even from his very bedding, but is otherwise devoted to the Muses and the Graces.

fixed: The glossary problem about 'the Graces' is not a real issue in the English: the English consistently uses 'the Graces' and 'the Muses' as proper names, matching the glossary. No change needed.
The glossary problem about 'the Muses' is not a real issue in the English: the English consistently uses 'the Muses' as a proper name, matching the glossary. No change needed.

last_rejected.quote: a soul with a pure plectrum sounding in varied response upon the tongue
last_rejected.source_quote: ψυχὴ καθαρῷ πλήκτρῳ ποικίλως ὑπηχοῦσα τῇ γλώττῃ
last_rejected.why: English makes 'soul' the subject of 'charms', but Greek has temple/precinct charming goddesses; soul is apposition/explanation.
last_rejected.fix: a soul with a pure plectrum making varied music upon the tongue
last_rejected.ruling: ψυχὴ...ὑπηχοῦσα is nominative apposition to preceding clause; English colon correctly separates it from 'charms' (θέλγει).

last_rejected.quote: the place where Dionysus was defeated by Ariadne and lived with her as her husband
last_rejected.source_quote: ἔνθα καὶ Διόνυσος τῆς Ἀριάδνης ἡττήθη καὶ σύνοικος ἦν
last_rejected.why: English omits 'καὶ' before Διόνυσος ('where also Dionysus'), losing the sense that Naxos is famed for this too.
last_rejected.fix: where also Dionysus was defeated by Ariadne
last_rejected.ruling: καὶ before Διόνυσος is a minor additive particle; 'the place where' adequately conveys the connection. Not a major loss.

last_rejected.quote: who dreams of taxes even from his very bedding
last_rejected.source_quote: κἀκ τῶν στρωμάτων αὐτῶν ὀνειροπολοῦντα τοὺς φόρους
last_rejected.why: αὐτῶν refers to 'his own' bedding, but 'very' overstates; more critically, κἀκ = 'even from', but the dream is OF taxes, not 'dreams of taxes from bedding'. The man dreams of taxes, with 'even from his bedding' indicating the extremity of his poverty.
last_rejected.fix: who even from his own bedding dreams of taxes
last_rejected.ruling: κἀκ τῶν στρωμάτων = 'even from their bedding'; ὀνειροπολοῦντα τοὺς φόρους = 'dreaming of taxes'. English accurately renders both.
